newsitem.title: USA: Blowouts a rising concern in deepwater U.S. Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Blowouts a rising concern in deepwater U.S. Gulf.

text.p: The race to explore deepwater oil and natural gas fields in the Gulf of Mexico has raised concerns about potential blowouts as producers stretch to reach reserves thousands of feet below the surface, industry experts said on Tuesday.

Of the 30 wells drilled in more than 3,000 feet of water in the Gulf of Mexico, four have been aborted as underground blowouts collapsed the geological hydrocarbon-bearing formations, well control engineer Larry Flak said.
"There were four short-term, underground blowouts," the Boots & Coots LP engineering manager said at an industry conference here. "They just lost the holes. There were no leaks," he said.

Oil companies have discovered 56 fields in water depths of up to 7,620 feet in the Gulf. By the year 2000, these deepwater fields are expected to boost daily production to between 1.66 million and 1.9 million barrels from the current rate of 945,000 barrels, according to federal regulators.

The promise of huge oil and gas reserves, along with reduced federal royalties on deepwater production, have sparked active bidding on deepwater leases and a resurgence in drilling in the Gulf of Mexico.

But to reach the deepwater reserves, producers have had to engineer complex systems for lowering drilling pipe through thousands of feet of turbulent water, controlling high pressures in the subsea fields and safely routing the oil and gas back to the surface.
A series of industry studies are underway as major producers active in the deepwater Gulf fields explore options for avoiding blowouts that potentially could result in disastrous oil spills.
"I think the industry is playing this game pretty well," said Flak, whose firm recently announced plans to merge with International Well Control to form Boots & Coots/IWC.

Although offshore producers Conoco, Petrobras, Amoco, Shell and Texaco's DeepStar consortium are studying well-control options, Flak said a veil of secrecy over deepwater projects could hamper efforts to understand the causes of future blowouts.
"A few operators are tight-lipped about close calls that they've had," he said.
